_comment: Hand-maintained annotations that a C header cannot express.
Everything inferable from alpm.h itself (string ownership via const-ness,
handle-ness via incomplete struct types, struct field layout) is NOT
recorded here -- emit.py derives it. This file is only for what clang
genuinely cannot see. Keep it small; if an entry could be a rule, make it
a rule.

rules._comment: Applied in order; first match wins. Overridden by 'functions'.

_comment: Accessors cheap enough to fetch for a whole list at once. They read a
field of an already-loaded db entry, so batching them is free; the
exclusions do real work (hashing a package file, computing a download
size) or are not accessors at all, and must stay one call per use.
Whether an accessor is cheap is not something the header states.
Calls after which a borrowed result the client has cached may be
stale, and which cached results those are. A setter replaces a
list, an add appends to it, a transaction rewrites the package
cache; after one of these the client detaches exactly the entries
named here, so the next read of one fetches afresh. Detached, not
freed -- after an add the old pointer is still valid memory
natively, and a caller may hold it -- and detached entries go when
the handle does, so naming only what can change is what keeps
that pile small.
`match` says which calls change anything. Each must get its keys:
from a `derive` rule -- the getter named like the setter, plural or
not, whichever exists -- or from an entry of its own here, or the
build fails. `under` is where the entries live: the first handle
argument (the default), everything under its root, or each element
of a named list argument. A key that is a regex names every getter
it matches. `columns` are batched package fields the call changes;
only a numeric one may be named, since a caller may hold a pointer
into a string column. coverage.json lists the outcome per call.

alpm_option_set_disable_dl_timeout.doc: Sets a scalar nothing caches, and libalpm has no getter for it, so the naming rule finds nothing; stated so that the check stays strict for the next setter.

alpm_db_unregister.doc: The db's own entries go with it (destroys); the handle's list of dbs is what is left to detach.

alpm_db_update.doc: libalpm throws away the package cache of each db it refreshed; which those were it does not say, so every db passed in is taken to have been.

alpm_trans_commit.doc: It is the local db's package cache that is rewritten, but the client does not know which db that is, so every db's goes; a sync db's is one round trip to fetch again.

_comment: alpm_list_t is untyped in C, so the element type of every list that
crosses the wire has to be stated. Getting one of these wrong is a
type confusion the compiler cannot catch, so they are grouped by
element type rather than alphabetically -- it makes a wrong entry
stand out.
Note the two compute_* functions return package NAMES, not packages,
despite their neighbours in this list returning alpm_pkg_t*.

param_list_elem._comment: Element type of alpm_list_t* parameters, same problem.

record_list_elem._comment: Element type of alpm_list_t* fields inside transparent structs, including the callback union variants.

alpm_initialize.doc: err is an out-param, not an input.

alpm_release.doc: Invalidates every handle owned by this alpm_handle_t.

alpm_errno.doc: What the stub returns when the server cannot be reached. The kind's default of zero would say ALPM_ERR_OK about a call that just failed.

alpm_strerror.doc: Never NULL, as libalpm's never is. With the server gone, the bridge's own reason is the most useful text there is, and it is what a frontend's error message then shows.

alpm_fetch_pkgurl.doc: urls goes in and fetched comes back. Its element type and its caller ownership were already stated; only the direction was missing.

alpm_db_unregister.doc: libalpm frees the db and its package cache; the id and everything under it go with them.

alpm_pkg_changelog_close.doc: Drops the cursor's id once libalpm has closed it. Unlike destroys, this releases one handle rather than an owner and everything under it.

skip._comment: Implemented by hand rather than generated, with the file each lives in. The callbacks used to be here; they are generated now, from the model plus the tag mappings in `callbacks` below.

_comment: Empty: the allowlist has served its purpose. Everything the emitter
can generate is now generated, and coverage.json says why the rest
is not.
These free a struct this client materialised, so they must never reach
the server -- it has libalpm's own copy, which it does not own. The
generated stub calls the matching free_<record> helper locally and costs
no round trip.
The value is the record whose free helper to call.
The same argument as client_local, one step short of it: the struct
itself belongs to the caller -- it was filled in place through an
out-param rather than returned -- so only its contents are released.
That is exactly what the generated clear_<record> does, and calling
libalpm's version would free the server's own copy instead.
Ownership of a returned struct pointer. Unlike strings, const-ness does
not settle this: both of these return a non-const pointer.
alpm_dep_from_string is documented as newly allocated and freed with
alpm_dep_free; alpm_db_get_group returns the db's own entry.
A `void *` that is not data but an object the server is holding open:
a cursor part-way through a changelog. The header says void, so
nothing in it can say which kind of object -- what is stated here is
the tag, which is what makes a stale or wrong-typed cursor fail a
lookup instead of reaching libalpm as a pointer.
The key is <function>.<param>, or <function>.@return.
mtree is deliberately not here. Its open and close would work exactly
like these, but alpm_pkg_mtree_next hands back a struct archive_entry
the client has no libarchive to read -- so declaring the cursor would
buy two thirds of an API nobody can use.
A buffer the caller provides and the callee fills, sized by another
parameter, with the number of bytes actually written as the return
value -- the read() shape. The server allocates its own, hands that to
libalpm, and the bytes travel back base64 like any other bytes here.
The value is the parameter holding the size.
Parameters that are n bytes and a length, not text. The header cannot
say so: `const unsigned char *` parses as a string, and sending one as
a string would stop at the first NUL, which a signature is full of.
`unsigned char **` parses as a string out-param and has the same
problem in reverse. What makes them tractable is that the length is
another parameter, and that is what is named here.
They travel base64, and the decoded length is the authority -- the
length that came alongside is checked against it, not trusted.
A variadic function whose `...` the client can format away, and the
name of the format parameter it formats into. The wire cannot carry
`...`, but the client is where the arguments are -- so it formats them
and the text travels. The server then calls libalpm with a literal
"%s" and that text, never with the text as the format.
This is the mirror of logcb, where the server consumes a va_list and
sends what it produced.
What a callback's signature cannot say. The setter, getter and ctx
getter are not restated here -- they are found in the model by type --
and the wire name is the setter's, minus alpm_option_set_ and cb.
The tagged unions are the whole difficulty. Which member is live
depends on a tag value, and C cannot write that down; getting it wrong
means reading a pointer out of a member libalpm never filled. Every
value of the tag enum has to appear here, mapped or in type_only, and
emit.py fails the build if one does not. That is what stops a variant
added in a later libalpm from arriving silently empty.
Where these mappings come from: alpm.h names the struct in its own doc
comment for six event types; hook, hook_run and pkg_retrieve are taken
from what pacman's frontend reads for them, since libalpm must fill
whatever the reference reader consumes. The DONE variants share their
START's member because hook.c reuses the struct it already populated.

alpm_cb_log.doc: The va_list cannot be marshalled, so the server consumes it into fmt and the text travels. args is a char* on Cygwin, which is exactly why this must be stated rather than inferred.

alpm_cb_question.doc: Every variant is {type, <answer>, ...payload}: the aliasing libalpm documents when it says `any` is always safe. emit.py checks that shape against each variant rather than trusting it.

alpm_cb_download.doc: Not a union: a void* whose type is named by a sibling argument, so libalpm states which it is passing instead of leaving a tag to be read out of the thing itself.

_comment: A count plus a pointer to N elements, rather than a pointer to one.
The field kinds cannot tell the difference -- `alpm_file_t *files` looks
exactly like a pointer to a single struct -- so which field holds the
count and which holds the array is stated here. The element type comes
off the array field, so it does not need saying twice.
These cross as a plain array; its length is the count.
Fields that do not cross, and why. A field named here is left zeroed
on the client instead of being filled with something wrong. That is
only acceptable because it is written down: coverage.json reports
every record that has one, so it cannot become a quiet way of calling
an awkward record supported.
alpm_pgpkey_t.data is the gpgme key object itself, and libalpm's own
fingerprint/uid/name/email point into it. A pointer into the server's
gpgme is meaningless here, and rebuilding an equivalent key would need
a gpg engine present in every caller's environment -- which would make
the field non-NULL only sometimes, and that is harder to reason about
than never. Everything a caller reads about the key is its own field
and crosses intact.
record_fields_uncarried._alpm_pgpkey_t.data: the gpgme key itself, which is the server's gpgme's to own

_comment: Records the materialiser must refuse rather than get wrong. Empty:
nothing in alpm.h is currently refused outright. Kept because the
next awkward record should land here rather than be forced through.
An out-list whose element type depends on why the call failed. The
header doc for alpm_trans_prepare names alpm_depmissing_t, but that
is only the unsatisfied-deps case: libalpm puts alpm_conflict_t there
for a conflict and package names for a bad arch, and pacman's own
sync_prepare() switches on alpm_errno() to tell which. The generated
code does the same on both sides, and the errno travels beside the
list. Every errno named here is checked against the enum; one not
named here arrives as an empty list, which is what libalpm leaves.
Calls after which libalpm has freed objects the handle table still
points at, and nothing in the header says so. Each is bracketed by a
pre and a post hook, hand-written in src/server/arpc_invalidate.c,
that note what is about to die and drop those ids afterwards. The
value says what dies.
server_hooks.alpm_trans_release: the packages loaded from files, and the copies made of the ones to remove
server_hooks.alpm_trans_commit: the installed version of every package it replaced or removed
server_hooks.alpm_db_update: the package cache of every db it refreshed
server_hooks.alpm_unregister_all_syncdbs: every sync db, with its package cache

_comment: An alpm_list_t** out-param is filled by libalpm and owned by the caller.
The server is that caller, so it frees its copy once serialised; the
client hands the caller a fresh list to free the documented way.
